turns.reply: Welcome, I'm glad you're here! Think of a time you snapped a biscuit in half or watched two drops of water run together on a window: what did you notice happening?

turns.student: um when i snap a biscuit it breaks into two pieces? and the water drops like merge together i guess
turns.reply: Yes, a biscuit breaking into two is the idea of splitting. Look at the diagram: a big uranium-235 nucleus takes in a tiny particle called a neutron, then splits into two smaller nuclei. If the two pieces came from one big nucleus, how many pieces do you get?
turns.diagramCaption: A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei. It gives out 2 or 3 neutrons.

turns.student: like three pieces? cus theres the neutron and then the two bits
turns.reply: Not quite. The neutron goes in first, then the big nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, like a biscuit snapping in half. The splitting itself is called nuclear fission. If a snapped biscuit gives you two pieces, how many smaller nuclei does one uranium-235 nucleus split into?

turns.student: oh right, two smaller nuclei then
turns.reply: When the nucleus splits, it also gives out 2 or 3 neutrons, and together the two smaller nuclei and those neutrons are called the fission products, like all the crumbs and pieces left after the snap. If the nucleus gives out 2 neutrons, how many fission products are there in total?

Fission products are just everything left over after the split, like all the pieces and crumbs once the biscuit snaps. They are the two smaller nuclei plus the neutrons that come out. If a nucleus gives out 3 neutrons, how many fission products come out altogether?

turns.student: um like 5? the two nuclei plus the 3 neutrons
turns.reply: Yes, 5 is right: the two nuclei plus the 3 neutrons. Uranium-235 is the fuel used in nuclear reactors, and it only splits after it absorbs a neutron, a bit like a biscuit that only snaps once you press on it. If a uranium-235 nucleus never meets a neutron, what would you expect it to do?

turns.student: it would just stay there and not split i guess
turns.reply: Yes, that's right: with no neutron to hit it, uranium-235 just stays as it is. Look at the diagram: each fission releases neutrons that can cause more fissions, and that repeating pattern is called a chain reaction. If one fission releases 3 neutrons and each of those causes another fission, how many fissions happen in the next step?
recap: Fission means a big nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, like snapping a biscuit.
Uranium-235 only splits after it absorbs a neutron, so no neutron means no split.
The split also gives out 2 or 3 neutrons.
The fission products are the two smaller nuclei plus those neutrons.
turns.diagramCaption: Each fission releases neutrons that can cause more fissions.

turns.reply: A chain reaction is when one fission sets off more fissions, like a row of dominoes where each one knocks over the next. Say one fission releases 3 neutrons, and each neutron hits a new nucleus and splits it. How many nuclei have split in that next step?

The answer is 3 nuclei split. Look at the diagram: in nuclear fusion, two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, and energy is released. Like your drops merging, what happens to two nuclei in fusion?
recap: Uranium-235 only splits when a neutron hits it.
Each fission releases neutrons that can trigger more fissions.
That repeating pattern is called a chain reaction, like falling dominoes.
One fission releasing 3 neutrons can lead to 3 new fissions next.
turns.diagramCaption: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, and energy is released.

turns.student: they join together to make one bigger nucleus
turns.reply: Yes, two nuclei joining into one bigger nucleus is exactly what fusion is. Fission and fusion are both nuclear reactions that release a lot of energy, but they work in opposite directions: fission splits one big nucleus, fusion joins two small ones. Which of the two is used in nuclear power stations today?
recap: In fusion, two light nuclei join to form one heavier nucleus.
Energy is released when the nuclei merge together.
Fusion is the opposite of fission, where a nucleus splits apart.

turns.reply:
Fair enough, I'll keep it short. Fission is the biscuit snapping, one big nucleus splitting apart. Fusion is the water drops merging, two small nuclei joining.

Which one of the two happens inside the Sun?

Fusion happens in the Sun, and stars like it. Fission usually starts when a big, unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron, and it's what nuclear power stations use today, with the chain reaction controlled so the energy comes out steadily. Fusion isn't used to make electricity on a large scale yet.

That's the end of this lesson. You answered questions on "Nuclear fission" and "Nuclear fusion", and I told you about "Chain reactions and controlling fission" and "Comparing fission and fusion". Thanks for sticking with it, and come back any time.
recap: Fission splits one big nucleus into smaller ones, releasing energy.
Fusion joins two small nuclei into one bigger nucleus, also releasing energy.
Fission is the biscuit snapping; fusion is two water drops merging.
The two reactions work in opposite directions but both release lots of energy.

turns.reply: Thanks for sticking with it. Today you answered questions on nuclear fission and nuclear fusion and I told you about chain reactions and controlling fission and comparing fission and fusion. Your progress is saved, so you can come back to this lesson any time. Bye for now!
